title: Lessons from the Trenches: Building LLM Evals That Work IRL: Aparna Dhinkaran
talk_summary: Arize co-founder Aparna Dhinakaran explains task evals for LLM applications: LLM-as-judge at multiple levels (router/function-call, span, trace, session), with explanations, built iteratively from real failures. She shows numeric judge scores are near-binary and unreliable, and that context placement and 'explain yourself first' prompting materially change retrieval/generation accuracy.

takeaways.technique: Evals with explanations, not bare scores
takeaways.what_they_do: LLM-as-judge returns a verdict plus a written explanation of what went wrong and where, so a human/agent can act on it instead of guessing from a number.
They corrupted documents at 80% vs 11% error density and asked judges to score severity; scores collapsed to 0/1/10 rather than tracking density.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it was either a one or it was a 10 but it was never like this linear range of scores
takeaways.numbers: 80% vs 11% corruption both scored 10; scores near-binary across foundation models

takeaways.technique: Component-level evals at each pipeline stage
takeaways.what_they_do: Instrument the app as a trace and put evals at the router/function-call level and inside each execution branch, so a wrong first decision is caught before downstream work is wasted.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the rest of the entire execution branch is going to be off because it got the first call wrong

takeaways.what_they_do: Every observed failure is added to a dataset, then prompt/function-description changes are validated by re-running experiments against that dataset.
takeaways.evidence_quote: every single time I get something wrong like this I'm going to go build up my data set and then use these to now eventually run experiments

takeaways.what_they_do: Needle-in-haystack tests across context sizes and depths show facts placed early in long contexts are retrieved worse; placement, not just inclusion, drives accuracy.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you put the fact earlier in the context window it actually had a really hard time almost remembering or retrieving
takeaways.numbers: Consistent 'red block' of retrieval failures early in the context window as context size grows

takeaways.what_they_do: Adding 'please explain yourself and then answer' to generation prompts produced a large accuracy jump for a model that was weak at generation despite strong retrieval.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we asked it to please explain yourself and then answer the question
takeaways.numbers: GPT-4 was ~4x worse than Claude 2.1 on generation tasks before the prompt change; 'remarkable jump' after
